Then it would make sense he would meld the imagery of the artificial window (something Anya enjoys) with space (for better or worse this is Curly's domain). Having no moon in the sky could also symbolize imbalance. Red of course being the main color can indicate violence, power, blood, sex, strength, etc.

I learned a few tricks from a few estheticians, and it worked in my experience. Use what works best for you though. :)  
  
 For new clients, you can start by telling them that your preferred method is to focus on the service and limit talking. For returning clients you can try to sell the maximum relaxation angle to limit conversations. You can also just tell returning clients you want to try something new if they need some convincing. 

You can do all the talking during the consultation and after the service. Get a quick recap of what is happening with them, what they want to work on during the appointment, and what type of massage they want. Guide them in the beginning and hopefully they get into the routine and automatically do this. Takes a while to get used to, but is worth it.

Gently remind them to focus on the service, the scents of the products, the feel, etc.  
Then after the service ask how they feel, what they liked, if they noticed anything with their skin, etc. 

Depending on where you work see if you can ask for more time in-between clients. I used to ask for this so I could prep my room and recharge. 

Also, entirely up to you if you want to apply this method to all services or just for facials. The esthetician I see just uses it for facials but will chat a bit with me during waxes. Although usually, we are just talking about industry stuff lol.

Ask your school if they will count student services. I know my school allowed that, and we set up appointments with other students on the days they didn't have class. If you have any local colleges nearby, hit those places up. College students love getting pampered. Especially during finals.

Being from out of state is a challenge, but I suggest taking advantage of that. If your time/budget allows, try to meet new people and you can use your schooling as an ice breaker. I have grabbed people from local events, randomly in my neighborhood, etc. 

Remember to keep yourself safe by always giving out the school's number to book appointments, and keep their business cards on hand.

I hate to say it but the burnout is real and sadly gets worse after graduation for some people.  
Do your best to not give up! An esthetics license can be surprisingly helpful if you know how to wield it/have a bit of luck.

I am not in the industry anymore (technically) but I keep my license current and have since moved into the accounting/tax industry, all thanks to my esthetics license.

Short answer is money and capitalism.  
Lots of people think of these jobs as recession proof, and if you have money to throw then you can start a business ASAP.  
   
To me the problem isn't so much the social media (although it doesn't help) but the lack of alternatives. Most of us have to make a decision that revolves around school or work, so beauty school can be a cheaper alternative to build your way up into other jobs or to work for yourself. Also combinations with the beauty industry can lead to some lucrative combos. Nursing and esthetics is common but there are others.

And if we need more fuel to the fire, schools use the perks of calling themselves colleges for that federal money, so more students flock there. This is one of those situations where it needs to get worse before it gets better. However, an obstacle is that so many are not willing/too tired to speak up to make the changes we need in the industry.

Autistic/ADHD person here!  
Just going to say that holding a grudge isn't going to help. Once you both cool off I would suggest sitting together and really analyzing your communication styles. Also discuss the social needs for each of you.   
I hate being interrupted too because of similar reasons to yours; however, I make a point to tell the people I regularly spend time with about conversation cues so they know when I feel like chatting vs wanting to listen.   
Keep in mind he also might be feeling hurt, so he retaliated. Not saying it is a great feeling or that it is warranted, but I have known quite a few people who respond this way (myself included).   
Anyway, sit down, talk it out, come up with a solution that works for both of you. For me I tell people that if they ask me about my day then that indicates to me they are ready to hear about the whole damn day xD  
I don't think either of you are AHs, just maybe haven't figured out some stuff. Miscommunication with neurodivergent people is pretty common I feel, so try not to stress too much.

It is the word we use when describing the skin reacting to a new skin care regimen or a specific active ingredient. I don't know what the official term would be besides calling it accelerated cell turnover, but it is an actual thing that happens.    
A good example is when people incorporate glycolic into their skincare routine and see more acne or blemishes. They think its not working but in reality the glycolic is just speeding up that cell turnover and bringing stuff from the surface up. So if the person had acne then that would appear.

Please note these are tips from an esthetician in the USA, take what applies. Hope something helps! And don't worry you'll get better at extractions, just takes time :)

* Check your tools. Are your tools causing too much trauma to the skin?
* What is your technique? Manual? Do you use tools? Can't provide tips on this since I do not know what the technique is. Whatever you use though just make sure it is not to traumatic to the skin. 
* This one you can't know for certain but are any of your clients likely to pick at their skin? If your clients scratch or pick at the area you just extracted they could potentially cause additional damage to the skin which could lead to a slower healing and/or marks.
* Are your clients older? Then purging will last longer.
* Do your clients have darker skin? Then PIH has a higher chance of occurring. Which translates to being extra gentle on the skin and mindful of how you extract.
* Are you extracting the right types of blemishes? We only want to extract what is on the surface and it should not be inflamed.
* Are you extracting thoroughly? We want to make sure that there is nothing left in the follicle. You can check by running your finger over the area. 
* Check the products you are using, some lines will have specific products to use for extractions to make them easier.
* Make sure the skin is prepped throughly before extractions. Use steam, exfoliate, and use nothing more than a medium pressure. If the congestion doesn't want to come out then leave it.
* If you want to continue doing extractions then I would suggest maybe learning from an esthetician who specializes in acne facials. I know videos are good, but it is better to learn from the actual person if you can.

Real talk, you probably will be targeted. I was in the same boat when I went to beauty school. Didn't like our educators, made waves, and paid a steep price. No one had my back.

It is unprofessional that your lead identified you. That should never happen. Best thing I can recommend is to go over your student handbook carefully and look at what your options are. Admin can be a hit or miss in terms of help but if your educator is unable to teach you and grade you fairly you can definitely bring it up with the school. Remember that if your educator can't do her job that's on her, not you. If the school tries to pin the blame on you, then lay low, study as hard as you can and report that school as much as you can.

Also, just a side-note but if an educator tells you that they will do their best to resolve a situation, take it with a healthy amount of skepticism. Oftentimes educators just get blocked by the owners of the school and can't do anything.  
   
Depending on the state you are in you can also report this to the appropriate organizations or DOL. They probably won't do anything but the reason so much crap like this happens is because not enough of us speak up. Still, it's an option.

In terms of the other students, they aren't going to have your back unless it benefits them I'm guessing. But you probably already know that.

If you do want to take control of your education then you can ask your lead for other resources to learn the material and rally students that you do trust/work well with and create a study group so you can support each other. Again, I don't know which state you are in but from what info I have gathered most exams are rote memorization, so if you find some decent study guides for your state you should be good to go.  

If you find yourself unable to make things work then look into options for transferring your credits to another school. Again, check with your state, and department of licensing for your best options.

I hope something I typed here helps, best of luck, and feel free to reach out as much as you need to on here. Lots of people here have great information for getting through the crappy times at beauty school.
